extracted.intended_audience: readers of literary criticism; aspiring writers, critics, and students of literature (Victorian/19th-century context)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying criteria for judging 'Heroes' (including Men of Letters) and literary worth — qualities such as sincerity, strength, originality, faith, practical prudence, and the relation of style to substance. Grounded in Carlyle's 19th‑century essayistic judgments and examples (Johnson, Burns, Rousseau, Bentham).

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization and public recognition of Men of Letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Society should provide some arrangement for the Literary Class — institutions, patronage or other means — so that literary talent can be discovered, tried, and put to use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle argues that literature's priesthood must be acknowledged and facilitated (e.g., France, Prussia show beginnings). Without public organization many apt men remain in garrets or perish as gaugers; proper season and assigner of money and station must be settled. The page cites the danger of leaving literary talent 'at the mercy of blind Chance' and contrasts worst (chaos, lost geniuses) with the desirable social regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial by the ordeal of Literary Life
rubrics_metrics.description: Genuine literary talent must 'pass through the ordeal' of literary life — struggle, poverty, and competition are part of proving merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle treats the 'wild welter' of literary life as an ordeal that tests men (Burns, Johnson examples). This struggle produces the strong men who constitute social progress. Antipattern: artificially sheltering talent from trial may fail to reveal who 'merits' reward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity / heart-sincerity
rubrics_metrics.description: A true writer or Hero is sincere — speaks and acts from the heart of Nature rather than by hearsay or cant; sincerity is the primary material of greatness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeatedly emphasized: 'the sincere man was by nature the obedient man'; Johnson's prophetic authority stems from speaking 'from the heart of Nature.' Antipatterns include cant, mere formulas without substance, and half-truths. Evidence of sincerity: consistent moral life, reverence, and words that 'mean things'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief (vs. scepticism) as a criterion of health
rubrics_metrics.description: Belief is defined as the healthy act of a man's mind; living by some genuine belief (not perpetual sceptical debate) is necessary for action and Heroism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle contrasts an 'Unbelieving Century'—moral and intellectual paralysis—with the necessity for belief to energize action. Scepticism is described as a chronic atrophy; while doubt and inquiry are natural, perpetual parading of doubt (making debate an end) is pathological. A writer's or hero's capacity to believe and act on belief is thus a key standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strength (calm endurance) over mere vehemence
rubrics_metrics.description: True greatness requires calm force, depth and the ability to endure heavy burdens; vehemence, convulsive fits of intensity, or loud passion are not equivalent to strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle praises 'the talent of Silence' and defines a strong man as one 'who can walk under the heaviest weight without staggering.' He criticizes Rousseau as intense but not strong, and warns that theatrical or convulsive energy is an inferior form of greatness. Scoring: prefer sustained, composed efficacy to explosive fervour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality as genuineness (not novelty)
rubrics_metrics.description: The essence of originality is not mere newness but being 'original' in the sense of being genuine, rooted in Nature — authenticity rather than novelty for novelty's sake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle: 'The essence of originality is not that it be new.' Johnson believed in old truths but was original because he 'stood by truth' with substance. Antipattern: valuing only the new or fashionable style while lacking substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substance over empty style; tolerating a 'tumed' style if it has content
rubrics_metrics.description: Style must carry substance; an ornate or tumid phraseology is tolerable if there is something within it, while beautiful style with nothing inside is condemnable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using Johnson as example: his 'wondrous buckram style' may be grandiloquent, but it has 'something within it.' Carlyle warns that many beautiful styles are empty and authors of such works are 'malefactors to the world.' Thus, when evaluating prose, check for inner truth and solidity before condemning stylistic heaviness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of Cant and Quackery
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear your mind of cant and avoid the simulacra of action — false benevolence, sentimentality, and public posturing that substitute for real work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle repeatedly condemns 'Cant,' 'Quacks,' and the 'similitude of Acting' that arises in a sceptical age. Example: Eighteenth‑century sentimental vaporing and public postures. Good practice: prioritize honest, useful action over ostentatious rhetoric or fashionable moralizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical moral prudence — act even when knowledge is limited
rubrics_metrics.description: In a world 'where much is to be done, and little is to be known,' one must emphasize practical moral prudence: decide how to act and do the work possible rather than be paralyzed by doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle names this Johnsonian Gospel as crucial: 'see how you will do it!' The standard privileges effective, earnest doing informed by a cleared mind rather than endless theoretical disputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrity, independence, and refusal of beggary
rubrics_metrics.description: A true man/writer should maintain independence and self-respect (refusing to beg), living honestly on what he can rightly obtain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Johnson's anecdote of the shoes thrown out the window: better to endure mud and cold honestly than beg. Evaluate character and life choices: integrity under privation ranks high. Antipattern: trading integrity for patronage or sham respectability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper relation of money/material support to artistic life
rubrics_metrics.description: Money can do much but cannot do all; it must be confined to its province and should not be the test of artistic worth — artistic life must be judged by spiritual standards as well as material support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle warns against believing financial rewards alone determine genius; but also notes the practical need to recognize and fund talent. Evaluation must balance acknowledging material constraints with prioritizing spiritual and sincere qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition and reverence of Heroes (worthy worship)
rubrics_metrics.description: Society (and individuals) should properly recognize and revere genuine excellence; worship of Heroes is natural and often right when the hero is truly noble.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Boswell's reverence for Johnson is praised as 'well bestowed.' Carlyle rebuts the aphorism 'no man is a hero to his valet' by arguing the valet's failure to perceive greatness is the valet's shortcoming. When assessing reputation, consider whether neglect stems from failure of perception rather than defect in the hero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti‑egoism: warn against vanity and hunger for praise
rubrics_metrics.description: Egoism (vain hunger for praise) is the source of many faults; true greatness should not be driven primarily by desire for reputation or applause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle diagnoses Rousseau's troubles as rooted in egoism and vanity. When evaluating an author's motive or character, look for signs of self-seeking versus selfless earnestness. Antipattern: overt self-promotion and clinginess to praise.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Talent of Silence' and timing of speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowing when to be silent and when to speak is a crucial mark of strength; premature or excessive emission of ideas (smoke) before they are matured (fire) is a fault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle counsels 'consume your own smoke' — work ideas into fire before publishing or proclaiming them. Rousseau is faulted for lacking this talent. Evaluate writers for restraint, depth, and the maturity of their expressed ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use intellect in practice — try those who have shown intellect
rubrics_metrics.description: Men who have shown intellectual capacity should be 'tried' in practical offices (e.g., government); demonstrated understanding is better tested by giving practical responsibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle cites Chinese practice of promoting promising scholars into governance as a model: try them even if untested in administration, because 'they have some Understanding.' This criterion applies where literary/intellectual gifts are being considered for leadership or public roles.
